subject: history_social
passage: Birch bark and palm leaf, the usual writing surfaces of early South Asia, rarely survive more than a few centuries, so most ancient texts from the region are known only through copies made long after the originals. That is why a discovery near Gilgit, in what is now northern Pakistan, has mattered so much to scholars. In 1931, local people found a cache of birch-bark Buddhist manuscripts inside the ruins of a stupa, where the dry mountain air had protected them for well over a thousand years. Some of the texts had previously been known mainly through Tibetan or Chinese translations. For these, the Gilgit manuscripts offer something no translation can: the Sanskrit wording itself, written down centuries before the copies scholars had relied on.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Dry mountain air protected the birch-bark manuscripts near Gilgit for over a thousand years.
choices.B: Tibetan and Chinese translations of Buddhist texts are less accurate than scholars once believed.
choices.C: Birch bark lasted longer than palm leaf as a writing surface in the dry regions of early South Asia.
choices.D: The Gilgit find gives scholars unusually early versions of texts otherwise known from later sources.

explanation.why: The text first explains a problem: most ancient South Asian texts survive only in much later copies. It then presents the Gilgit manuscripts as valuable because they are very old and, for some texts, preserve the original Sanskrit wording that was otherwise known mainly through translations. The main idea is the significance of the find as an early source.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The dry air explains how the manuscripts survived, but this detail leaves out why the find matters.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says only that translations cannot show the original wording; it never judges their accuracy.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text groups birch bark and palm leaf together as surfaces that rarely survive; it does not compare them.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the whole argument: the find matters because it preserves early versions of texts that otherwise survive mainly in later copies or translations.
